analysis.one_liner: Shifts the cost of cleaning up packaging and single-use plastics onto the companies that make them.
analysis.headline: The bill won 130 Democratic cosponsors but never got a hearing markup or a vote in the House before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make companies that sell packaged goods, beverages, and food service products pay to collect, recycle, or compost them after consumers are done. It sets rising recycling and recycled-content targets, phases out many single-use plastic items, puts a 10-cent minimum deposit on beverage containers that consumers get back when they return the container, and pauses new permits for facilities that make plastics until pollution rules catch up. It also bans exporting plastic waste to countries with weaker standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit through less plastic litter in waterways and communities, fewer toxic chemicals like PFAS and phthalates in food packaging, a 10-cent refund on every returned beverage can or bottle, and shifting recycling costs from municipal taxpayers to the companies whose products create the waste.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes producers financially responsible for collecting, managing, and recycling or composting their products after consumer use, shifting costs that now fall on local governments and taxpayers [S2].
Consumers would receive a refund of at least 10 cents for returning beverage containers, and states with existing bottle laws would be updated to match [S3].

It would phase out many single-use plastic items such as plastic utensils and carryout bags beginning January 1, 2023, while requiring businesses to provide plastic straws to any customer who requests one [S2][S3].
It would impose a temporary moratorium on new or expanded permits for certain plastics manufacturing facilities until regulations address pollution from those facilities [S2].
It bans exporting plastic waste to countries without equivalent health and environmental standards, stopping the practice of shipping US plastic waste abroad [S2][S3].
Companies with under $1 million in annual revenue and small retailers are exempt from the main producer-responsibility requirements and face limited penalties [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Packaging manufacturers, beverage companies, and consumer goods producers would pay new fees to Producer Responsibility Organizations covering collection, recycling, cleanup, and EPA oversight costs; the plastics industry would face a permit moratorium; restaurants and retailers would bear the bag, utensil, and container take-back rules. Some costs would be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Producer fees and bottle deposits would raise the cost of everyday goods for shoppers, and the 10-cent deposit applies at purchase even though consumers only get it back if they return the container [S3].

The bill waives antitrust laws for companies coordinating through Producer Responsibility Organizations, allowing competitors to jointly plan fees and operations if needed to implement their plans [S3].

Recycling targets of 65-90 percent by 2032 may be unrealistic given current US processing capacity, risking compliance costs or adjustments; the bill itself defines recyclable by whether processing capacity actually exists [S3].
The plastics permit moratorium could delay investment and jobs in the petrochemical sector while regulators update pollution rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The environmental and public-health benefits are broad: less plastic in waterways, fewer toxic chemicals in packaging, lower cleanup costs for local governments, and money back on returned containers. The costs are real and concentrated — companies would pay significant fees, and part of that would show up in prices and deposits for consumers. The bill's small-business exemptions and refundable deposit design moderate the burden on ordinary households, and the main honest objection is whether the recycling infrastructure exists to hit the bill's targets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in four House committees for the rest of the two-year Congress; its subcommittees held one hearing in June 2022, but no committee ever voted to send it to the House floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced March 26, 2021 by Rep. Alan Lowenthal with 88 original cosponsors and referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Foreign Affairs Committees [S1][S3][S5].
It gathered 130 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].

On March 29, 2021 it was referred to two subcommittees, and the subcommittees held a hearing on June 30, 2022, but no committee markup or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended January 3, 2023 [S5].
No companion vote was held in the Senate and the bill never received a roll call in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaging, beverage, and plastics producers are better off because the bill never advanced: they avoid producer fees, recycled-content mandates, take-back obligations, and the moratorium on new plastics plant permits. Local governments and taxpayers continue to pay for managing and cleaning up plastic waste.

for.name: Rep. Alan Lowenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 130 cosponsors for a national extended-producer-responsibility program for packaging and plastics.

for.name: 130 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat and none was a Republican.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral (Chair Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 26, 2021, held one subcommittee hearing on June 30, 2022, and never marked up or reported the bill to the full House.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Foreign Affairs Committees
against.what_they_did: Never took up or reported the provisions referred to them during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 130 cosponsors were Democrats and none was a Republican; no vote was ever held, so the full chamber's position was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would impose a moratorium on new or expanded permits for certain plastics manufacturing facilities until pollution rules are updated, and restricts exports of plastic waste. The industry gains nothing from the bill's failure except keeping the status quo, in which taxpayers fund cleanup of plastic pollution.

industries.industry: Beverage companies and beverage container makers
industries.note: They would have to collect deposits, hit 25-80 percent recycled-content mandates for plastic bottles, and fund take-back infrastructure through producer fees. Because the bill died, these costs stayed off their books and continued to fall on municipal waste systems.

Extended producer responsibility would make them pay for collecting, recycling, and cleaning up their products, with fees scaled to how hard their designs are to recycle. The death of the bill preserves the current system where local governments bear those costs.

industries.industry: Recycling, composting, and waste collection industry
industries.note: Producer-funded programs must spend at least half their first-decade budgets building US recycling and composting infrastructure and pay collection providers 100 percent of management costs. With the bill dead, this market expansion never materialized.

They would face bans on single-use plastic bags, utensils, and polystyrene, and take-back duties for bottles and containers, but businesses under $1 million in annual revenue are exempt from the main requirements and get capped penalties. Larger chains would bear most compliance costs, which can be passed to shoppers.
